title: Neuromuscular consequences of an extreme mountain ultra-marathon
authors: Millet GY, Tomazin K, Verges S, Vincent C, Bonnefoy R, Boisson RC, Gergele L, Feasson L, Martin V
population: Experienced ultra-marathon runners, 166 km mountain race with 9500 m positive and negative elevation change; 22 tested immediately post, 11 followed to day 16
findings: Maximal voluntary contraction fell -35% (95% CI -28 to -42%) in knee extensors and -39% (-32 to -46%) in plantar flexors immediately after the race; maximal voluntary activation fell -19% (-7 to -32%), mainly in knee extensors.
Creatine kinase rose from 144 +/- 94 to 13,633 +/- 12,626 U/L, myoglobin from 32 +/- 22 to 1,432 +/- 1,209 ug/L, CRP from <2.0 to 37.7 +/- 26.5 mg/L.
Excitation-contraction coupling was impaired (low frequency fatigue, reduced high-frequency doublet force and compound muscle action potential amplitude) in both muscle groups.

Tested before, immediately after and at 2, 5, 9 and 16 days (n = 11 for follow-up): neuromuscular function had returned to initial values 16 days after the race, with most of the recovery occurring within 9 days.
limitations: Only 11 runners completed follow-up testing (self-selected, experienced, a single race); no running-load control during recovery; the abstract reports no day-by-day numbers for the recovery tests, only the 9-day and 16-day statements.
implications: For a 100 km and 100-mile race, treat neuromuscular recovery as a roughly two-week process: most of it by about day 9, complete by day 16. A return schedule that reaches full training load before about day 14 is not supported by objective function data.

Keep intensity, downhill and plyometric loading out of the first 9 days after a 100-mile race; the data do not say what running load is safe within that window, so the hold itself rests on convention (see the coach pages) plus this time course.
Because only the 9-day and 16-day points are reported as recovery milestones, the engine should not claim finer resolution than that for the ramp.
